pronunciation.respelling: kan eye GET uh larj eyest KAW-fee pleez
pronunciation.text: Americans pronounce the r in «large». The t in «get a» is soft, nearly «geddə», and «iced» ends in a clear t.

mnemonic.title: «Here» or «go»
mnemonic.text: Two tiny words sum it up: «here» means you stay and drink from a mug, «go» means you walk out with a paper cup. Americans say «to go»; British speakers say «to take away».

grammar.title: Short questions
grammar.text: Counter staff drop the opening words: «For here or to go?» means «Is it for here, or to go?». Your answer can be just «To go, please» or «For here».

pronunciation.title: Two big beats
pronunciation.text: Stress «here» and «go»; the little words «for», «or» and «to» shrink to «fer», «er» and «tuh». The vowel in «go» is a glide: oh-oo.

target: Can I get oat milk instead?

translations.bg-BG: Може ли овесено мляко вместо това?
translations.ru-RU: Можно мне овсяное молоко вместо обычного?
translations.pl-PL: Czy mogę prosić mleko owsiane zamiast zwykłego?
translations.cs-CZ: Můžu dostat ovesné mléko místo obyčejného?

mnemonic.title: Oat rhymes with boat
mnemonic.text: Picture a little boat floating in a cup of creamy oat milk: «oat» rhymes with «boat».

grammar.title: «Instead» at the end
grammar.text: «Instead» comes at the end and swaps one thing for another: «oat milk instead» means «instead of the regular milk». No extra words needed.

pronunciation.title: Oat = boat
pronunciation.respelling: kan eye GET oht milk in-STED
pronunciation.text: «Oat» has the long «oh» of «boat», ending in a crisp t. Stress «instead» on its second syllable: in-STED.

mnemonic.title: Any card is «credit»
mnemonic.text: In the US almost any bank card is a «credit card» in everyday speech. Picture swiping a card at the register and just say «credit».

grammar.title: «Do you take…?»
grammar.text: «Do you take…?» asks what a shop accepts: «Do you take cards?», «Do you take cash?». It works in any shop, with a plural noun.

pronunciation.title: Crisp d, buzzing z
pronunciation.text: «Credit» has a clear d and a weak middle «i». Pronounce the r in «cards» and end with a voiced z, not an s.

mnemonic.title: Sub + way
mnemonic.text: «Sub» means under and «way» is a road: a «subway» is the road under the city. In Britain «subway» is just a pedestrian underpass; the train is the «tube» or «underground».

grammar.title: «Where's…?»
grammar.text: «Where's» is «where is», the quick way to ask for a place: «Where's the station?», «Where's the restroom?». Add the place after it.

pronunciation.title: Two stresses
pronunciation.text: Stress «sub» and «sta»; «the» shrinks to «thuh». Say «-tion» as «shun».

translations.bg-BG: Този влак отива ли в центъра?
translations.pl-PL: Czy ten pociąg jedzie do centrum?

mnemonic.title: Down + town
mnemonic.text: Picture a city on a hill with the busy centre at the bottom: you go «down» to the «town». In the US «downtown» is the city centre; British speakers say «town centre».

grammar.title: Present tense for schedules
grammar.text: «Does this train go…?» uses the simple present for fixed routes. After «does», the verb stays plain: «go», never «goes».

pronunciation.title: Down-TOWN
pronunciation.text: In «downtown» the stress falls on the second half: down-TOWN. The «ow» is the vowel of «now», and the final n is clear.

target: Can you take me to the airport?

translations.bg-BG: Можете ли да ме закарате до летището?
translations.ru-RU: Вы можете отвезти меня в аэропорт?

mnemonic.title: Cab = taxi
mnemonic.text: Short and snappy like a ride: «cab» is the American word for «taxi», and this sentence suits a cab driver and a rideshare driver alike.

grammar.title: «Can you take me to…?»
grammar.text: «Take me to» plus a place is all you need: «Can you take me to the airport?». For an address, just say it.

pronunciation.title: AIR-port
pronunciation.ipa: [kæn ju teɪk mi tu ði ˈɛrˌpɔrt]
pronunciation.respelling: kan yoo TAYK mee too thee AIR-port
pronunciation.text: Stress «air»: AIR-port. Before a vowel «the» becomes «thee». The r in «airport» is pronounced.

target: Go two blocks and turn left

translations.bg-BG: Минете две пресечки и завийте наляво
translations.ru-RU: Пройдите два квартала и поверните налево
translations.pl-PL: Przejdź dwie przecznice i skręć w lewo
translations.cs-CZ: Jděte dvě křižovatky a odbočte vlevo

mnemonic.title: A block is a chunk of street
mnemonic.text: A «block» is one chunk of street between two crossings, like a block of cheese in a grid. Americans count distance in blocks, not metres.

grammar.title: Commands without «you»
grammar.text: Directions use the plain verb: «Go», «turn». No «you» needed. Join steps with «and»: «Go two blocks and turn left».

pronunciation.title: Blocks and turn
pronunciation.respelling: goh too BLOCKS and TURN left
pronunciation.text: «Blocks» ends in ks, and «and» shrinks to «n» in speech. The American «ur» in «turn» is one r-coloured vowel, no separate r.

translations.bg-BG: Къде е щандът за плодове и зеленчуци?
translations.pl-PL: Gdzie jest dział z owocami i warzywami?
translations.cs-CZ: Kde je oddělení ovoce a zeleniny?

mnemonic.title: Produce comes from farms
mnemonic.text: Think «pro-duce»: what farms «produce», fruit and vegetables. That is the word on the sign over the section.

grammar.title: «Section»
grammar.text: «Section» names a part of a store: «the produce section», «the dairy section». Ask «Where's…?» with any of them.

pronunciation.title: PRO-duce
pronunciation.text: The noun «produce» is stressed on the first syllable: PROH-doos. The verb is pro-DOOCE; the sign over the section is the noun.

mnemonic.title: Two bags
mnemonic.text: Picture the two bags at the checkout: crinkly brown «paper» and shiny «plastic». The cashier's whole question is just those two nouns.

grammar.title: A choice of two nouns
grammar.text: A question can be just two nouns joined by «or». The word «bag» is understood, so «Paper or plastic?» means «Paper bag or plastic bag?». Answer with one word: «Paper, please».

pronunciation.title: Two stresses
pronunciation.text: Stress the first syllable of both nouns: PAY-per, PLAS-tik. The end of «paper» is the weak r-vowel «er», and «or» shrinks to «er».

mnemonic.title: Cart, not trolley
mnemonic.text: Picture a big metal «cart» rolling across a huge American parking lot. British shoppers call it a «trolley».

grammar.title: «Where are…?» for plurals
grammar.text: Use «Where are…?» for plural things: «Where are the carts?». For one thing it is «Where's…?» (where is).

pronunciation.title: Open o, strong r
pronunciation.text: In «shopping» the o is a wide «ah», like in «father». Pronounce the r in «carts» and end with ts.

target: Do you have a rewards card?

mnemonic.title: A reward for coming back
mnemonic.text: A «reward» is a prize for coming back: picture the store handing you a gold star each time. The cashier asks this at nearly every American supermarket.

grammar.title: Yes/no with «Do you…?»
grammar.text: Questions with «Do you have…?» start with «Do» and need no change to the verb. Answer «Yes, I do» or «No, I don't»; saying no is perfectly fine.

pronunciation.title: Re-WARDS
pronunciation.respelling: doo yoo hav uh ri-WORDZ kard
pronunciation.text: Stress the second syllable: ri-WORDZ, ending in a voiced z. In fast speech «do you» runs together as «dya».

target: Hi, I'm Anna. Nice to meet you!

translations.bg-BG: Здравей, аз съм Анна. Приятно ми е!
translations.pl-PL: Cześć, jestem Anna. Miło mi cię poznać!

mnemonic.title: A handshake
mnemonic.text: Picture a handshake: «meet» is two people coming together, and «nice» is the smile that goes with it.

grammar.title: «I'm» + name
grammar.text: «I'm» is «I am». Say «I'm Anna» to give your name; it is shorter and friendlier than «My name is Anna», which is also correct.

pronunciation.title: Nice to MEET you
pronunciation.ipa: [haɪ aɪm ˈænə naɪs tə mit ju]
pronunciation.respelling: hy eyem AN-uh nys tuh MEET yoo
pronunciation.text: Stress «meet»: nys tuh MEET yoo. «To» weakens to «tuh», and «meet you» can blend into «mee-chu».

mnemonic.title: A journey
mnemonic.text: Picture a road trip: «going» is how the journey is moving. Americans say this instead of «hello», and do not wait for a long answer.

grammar.title: A greeting, not a question
grammar.text: «How's it going?» is «How is it going?» squeezed into a greeting. Answer short: «Good, you?» or «Pretty good, thanks». British speakers often say «All right?» instead.

pronunciation.title: Howz-it GOH-ing
pronunciation.text: The first two words blur into «howz-it»; stress «go». The «ing» ending is quick, with a soft ng.

mnemonic.title: A map with a pin
mnemonic.text: Picture a map with a pin: «from» points back to the place where someone started. It is the most common question after hello.

grammar.title: «From» stays at the end
grammar.text: In «Where are you from?» the word «from» stays at the end; never move it to the front. The answer repeats it: «I'm from Poland».

pronunciation.title: Two stressed words
pronunciation.text: Stress «where» and «from». The vowel in «from» is a short «uh»; pronounce the r in «where» and «are».

translations.bg-BG: Да пием по едно кафе някой път.

mnemonic.title: Grab = snatch
mnemonic.text: Picture quickly grabbing a cup on the way: «grab coffee» means a short, casual meet-up, not a big plan.

grammar.title: «Let's» + verb
grammar.text: «Let's» is «let us» and suggests something together: «Let's grab coffee», «Let's go». The verb after it stays plain.

pronunciation.title: The flat a
pronunciation.text: «Grab» has the flat «a» of «cat». The first vowel of «coffee» is an open «aw», and «sometime» is stressed on «some».

target: Can we get a table for two?

translations.pl-PL: Czy możemy dostać stolik dla dwóch osób?

mnemonic.title: A table for two
mnemonic.text: Picture a table set with two plates: «for two» says how many chairs. At a busy US restaurant you wait at the front for the host to seat you.

grammar.title: Numbers after «for»
grammar.text: «A table for two» names the group size: «for three», «for four». It works in any restaurant, and «Can we get…?» is the polite everyday request.

pronunciation.title: Soft t, dark l
pronunciation.ipa: [kæn wi ɡɛt ə ˈteɪbəl fɔr tu]
pronunciation.respelling: kan wee GET uh TAY-bul for TOO
pronunciation.text: The t in «get a» flaps to a quick «d». «Table» ends in a dark, swallowed «l»: TAY-bul.

mnemonic.title: A room to rest
mnemonic.text: A «rest-room» is a room to rest: picture a quiet little room with a sink. Americans say «restroom» or «bathroom», almost never «toilet».

grammar.title: A polite word choice
grammar.text: In the US «toilet» means just the fixture, so ask for the «restroom» (public places) or the «bathroom» (homes). British speakers say «toilet» or «loo».

pronunciation.title: REST-room
pronunciation.text: Stress «rest»: REST-room. The «oo» in «room» is long.

target: Can we get the check, please?

mnemonic.title: A tick in the box
mnemonic.text: Picture ticking a box: the «check» is the slip you check over before paying. Americans ask for the «check», British speakers for the «bill».

grammar.title: «The» check
grammar.text: Say «the check», not «a check»: there is one bill for the table. Waiters bring it when you ask, so asking is polite and normal.

pronunciation.title: Ch as in cheese
pronunciation.respelling: kan wee GET thuh CHEK pleez
pronunciation.text: «Check» starts with «ch» as in «cheese» and ends with a crisp k. Keep the z in «please» voiced.

mnemonic.title: A little extra
mnemonic.text: A «tip» is a little extra for good service, a small «tip» of your hat to the waiter. In the US it is a normal part of the meal, usually 15–20%.

grammar.title: Flip the order for questions
grammar.text: To ask a yes/no question with «is», put it first: «The tip is included» becomes «Is the tip included?». Asking is practical and never rude.

pronunciation.title: in-KLOO-did
pronunciation.text: Stress the middle: in-KLOO-did. The ending «-ed» is a separate syllable here, «did», because the verb stem ends in d.
